attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his Substack post, stated in his own voice.

semantics.note: The unqualified 'I expect' about a definite pattern makes this a scored forecast. The separate present-tense remark that China is 'at most a few months behind' is rightly left out. No deadline was stated.

contract.note: Measuring the lead with capability indices and treating 'flip back and forth' as repeated changes at the top is an ordinary reading. 'Slight', 'sizeable' and 'for long' are not quantified, so the result depends on interpretation, and the contract flags this.

evidence.note: Epoch ECI data up to Jan 2026: the US held the frontier the whole time and China trailed by 4–14 months. Nearly all of it predates the Dec 2025 post, so it cannot settle a pattern that should play out after the post.

reviews.rationale: This is a scored forecast with no deadline. The only evidence is Epoch's record ending a few weeks after the post. It shows no flips before the post, but it does not cover the period the forecast is about. No multi-year record after the post exists in the packet, so the early-resolution rule is not met.

attribution.note: Marcus's own sentence in his post.

semantics.note: A present-tense description of the market, built on an analogy. The surrounding text ('largely similar products', 'nobody has a real technical advantage') supports reading it as a factual claim that the products are interchangeable.

contract.note: The plain reading (interchangeable products, choice mainly on price, prices pushed toward cost) is the ordinary business sense of 'commodity'. The Coke/Pepsi comparison loosens it somewhat, which the contract flags. The reading is fair, but the result depends on it.

evidence.note: Epoch, Mar 2025, inside the target period: the price of a fixed capability level fell 9x–900x per year. That fits commodity-like competition once a capability is matched.

Menlo survey, mid-2025: builders choose frontier models and pay for performance rather than price. This meets the contract's contradiction condition. Menlo is a venture investor, so it is not fully neutral.
Same report: only 11% of builders switched vendors, and most stayed with their provider. That points to loyalty, although the report also calls switching relatively easy.

reviews.rationale: One part holds: prices at a fixed capability fell steeply (e1), and switching is described as easy. The other part fails: buyers mainly chose on performance, paid for frontier models and stayed with their providers (e2, e3), which is what the contract's contradiction condition describes. So the market looks like a commodity at fixed capability, but not at the frontier.

attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his post.

semantics.note: It combines a present-tense observation ('is not') with a never-type forecast ('will not ever be'). The forecast part has no deadline and is what the contract scores.

contract.note: Reading 'winner take all' as one country or firm taking essentially the whole market and excluding rivals matches the speaker's own gloss ('to the exclusion of the other'). The one-sided early-resolution rule suits a never-type forecast.

evidence.note: Mid-2025 snapshot: US enterprise LLM use was split among several firms (Anthropic 32%, OpenAI 25%). It predates the post, says nothing about China, and cannot settle 'ever'.

reviews.rationale: This is a never-type forecast with no deadline. Nothing in the packet shows one country or firm taking essentially the whole market, so the contract's early-contradiction rule is not met, and a forecast of this kind cannot be confirmed early. The only evidence is a snapshot from before the post.

attribution.note: Marcus's own parenthetical remark in his post.

semantics.note: A universal ('never') present-tense description of how long leads last among US labs, bounded by 'a few months'.

contract.note: Measuring the lead on the Arena leaderboard and applying 'never' to the period since public leaderboards began (2023) is an ordinary reading of an absolute word. If 'never' meant only the 2025 pattern, the result would change. The contract flags this.

evidence.note: Ars Technica: versions of OpenAI's GPT-4 held #1 on Chatbot Arena from about May 2023 to March 2024, roughly 10 months. That is clearly more than a few months.
Gemini 2.5 Pro took #1 in Mar 2025, the start of a run of about 4.5 months. That fits the claim for 2025 only.
GPT-5 took #1 in Aug 2025, ending Google's run after about 4.5 months. Consistent with the claim for 2025.
Gemini 3 Pro took #1 in Nov 2025, about 3.5 months after GPT-5. Consistent with the claim for 2025.
This shows Anthropic's lasting share of enterprise coding use. That is market share, not the capability lead the contract measures.

reviews.rationale: The claim is universal ('never'). GPT-4 held #1 on Arena for about 10 months in 2023–24 (e1), which meets the contract's contradiction condition. The 2025 runs of 3.5–4.5 months (e2–e4) fit the pattern for that year, but they cannot rescue the universal claim.
